profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting in an ML research lab the morning after an internal reproduction run of a 'multiplication-free' ResNet-18 training method failed to match the paper's reported CIFAR-100 accuracy. The team has a branch that replaces floating-point multiply with an integer-add-based surrogate inside custom CUDA kernels for convolution and linear layers, and the overnight runs plateaued 6-8 points below the lab's FP32 baseline while showing occasional loss spikes after epoch 120. The meeting is between the PhD researcher who adapted the method into the lab's vision training stack and the research engineer who integrated and instrumented the custom kernels. Their agenda is to diagnose whether the gap comes from the arithmetic substitution itself, a mismatch between their setup and the paper-aligned recipe, or an execution-path issue, and to agree on the smallest follow-up test to run today. The expected outcome is one concrete root-cause hypothesis and a tightly scoped action plan for a single rerun with better logging.

members.name: Dr. Lina Park
members.expertise: deep learning optimization, reproduction of training methods, vision benchmarking
members.background: Lina is a fourth-year PhD candidate who owns the lab's ResNet training recipes for CIFAR and ImageNet-style experiments and regularly ports academic methods into the group's PyTorch stack for reproduction studies.
members.private_state: She wants to preserve the interpretation that the arithmetic idea itself is viable and worries the current miss will be dismissed as a failure of the method rather than as recipe drift or a narrow implementation mismatch; she also wants to avoid opening a broad systems audit before next week's group review.
hidden_assumptions: When discussing whether the method is 'multiplication-free,' the scientifically relevant scope for this troubleshooting pass is the learned layer math in convolution and linear forward/backward passes, because that is where the paper's contribution lives.
When someone says 'baseline recipe' or 'same setup,' they naturally mean the lab's current CIFAR training template unless someone explicitly says they reverted to the older paper-aligned defaults.
A run is still 'stable' if it trains to completion and the final accuracy trajectory remains usable, even when there are a few late isolated spikes.
Saying the run stayed on the 'custom kernel path' ordinarily refers to the training loop's main forward/backward path for standard minibatches, since that is what determines optimization behavior.

members.name: Ethan Morales
members.expertise: CUDA extensions, numeric execution tracing, PyTorch kernel dispatch and determinism
members.background: Ethan is a research engineer who maintains the lab's custom PyTorch extensions and recently added the integer-add surrogate into fused convolution and GEMM kernels, along with lightweight dispatch logging to check where the custom path is actually exercised.
members.private_state: He wants to determine whether the disappointing result reflects a real numeric issue in the kernelized arithmetic path or a misleading comparison caused by setup drift, and he is particularly concerned that an incomplete execution audit could lead them to make claims about the method that are not actually supported by what ran.
hidden_assumptions: When they call the experiment 'multiplication-free training,' the phrase should at least mean that every operation central to the claimed substitution in learned layers truly avoids hardware multiply instructions, with no unnoticed fallback inside those conv/GEMM execution paths.

When people say 'the paper setup' or 'baseline recipe,' they are referring to the originally paper-aligned augmentation and evaluation settings used when this reproduction effort began, not the lab's later template defaults.

A run should only be called 'stable' if the loss and gradient behavior remain smooth enough that the surrogate arithmetic is not introducing intermittent numeric pathologies, even if the job technically finishes.

Checking the 'custom kernel path' means verifying execution coverage anywhere the reported accuracy depends on that path, including validation/eval forwards and edge-case shapes such as the final short batch, not only the standard training minibatches.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss whether the run is really 'multiplication-free.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the key learned-layer computations under study—convolution and linear forward/backward math—used the integer-add surrogate instead of floating-point multiplication, so the experiment is faithful enough for troubleshooting the paper's core claim.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the claim is only trustworthy if the conv/GEMM arithmetic path itself is comprehensively multiply-free in actual execution, including any fused sub-steps or silent dispatch fallback within those learned-layer kernels, rather than merely replacing the obvious top-level multiply sites in code.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are talking about the same custom-kernel branch and both know optimizer and batch-norm math were not rewritten, so the phrase 'multiplication-free' sounds shared and practical; the disagreement is only about how strict the execution boundary must be inside the learned-layer path, which feels too obvious to unpack.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to compare against the 'baseline recipe' or 'paper setup.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means the lab's current ResNet/CIFAR recipe template, including its newer crop policy, label smoothing default, and current reporting flow.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means the older paper-aligned reproduction setup from the project's start, with the original augmentation defaults and simpler evaluation procedure.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both recipes live in the same codebase and are both familiar to the team, so saying 'baseline recipe' feels fully specific in conversation even though each silently anchors to a different historical default.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They assess whether the overnight run was 'stable.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 judges stability by whether training completes without collapse and ends in a competitive enough accuracy range despite a few late spikes.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 judges stability by whether the loss curve and gradient norms remain smooth enough that the arithmetic substitution is not causing rare numeric disruptions, even if final accuracy is only moderately affected.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML troubleshooting, 'stable' is common shorthand for 'basically not broken,' so both can use the same word cooperatively while applying different implicit thresholds for what qualifies.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to verify the 'custom kernel path'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer to confirming that the run stayed on the 'custom kernel path.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the standard training forward/backward passes for full-size minibatches, where the optimization signal is generated.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of all accuracy-relevant execution points, especially the validation forward path and odd-shape cases like the final incomplete batch that may dispatch differently from the main training loop.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase points to the same code branch and logging machinery, so it sounds concrete and shared; the hidden divergence is about which specific invocations count as 'the path' worth verifying, and that boundary is rarely spelled out in a quick troubleshooting meeting.
